Chapter 2 · 第二章

How to Become a Tech Lead如何成为技术负责人

— PDF p.49 —

Becoming a tech lead is an exciting but challenging transition. This chapter will guide you through the journey of stepping into the role, building the skills you need, and overcoming common obstacles along the way.

成为技术负责人是一次令人兴奋却充满挑战的转型。本章将带你走过这段旅程：走上这个岗位、搭建所需的技能，并克服沿途常见的障碍。

First, I'll explore how to set a strong foundation for your growth by adopting the right mindset and understanding the importance of intentional development. Then, I'll walk through creating and implementing a growth plan tailored to your unique context and goals. Finally, I'll emphasize the importance of reflecting on your progress and making adjustments to stay aligned with your objectives.

首先，我会探讨如何通过树立正确的心态、理解“有意识成长”的重要性，为你的成长打下坚实基础。接着，我会带你制定并执行一份量身定制、契合你自身处境与目标的成长计划。最后，我会强调复盘进展、持续调整以确保方向不偏离目标的重要性。

Once your growth strategy is in place, I'll address common challenges that new tech leads face. Time management often becomes difficult to balance, so I'll explore how to effectively plan and manage your new responsibilities. I'll also cover strategies for avoiding the “therapist trap,” where you might feel pressured to solve everyone's problems, and how to steer clear of micromanaging your team. Finally, I'll dive into finding the right balance between hands-on coding and providing technical oversight, a delicate but essential aspect of the tech lead role.

成长战略就位之后，我会聊聊新任技术负责人常遇到的挑战。时间管理往往变得难以平衡，因此我会探讨如何有效地规划并管理这些新职责。我还会介绍如何避开“治疗师陷阱”——在那种状态下你会感到有压力去解决每个人的问题——以及如何避免对团队进行微观管理。最后，我会深入探讨如何在亲自动手写代码与提供技术把控之间找到恰当的平衡，这是技术负责人角色中微妙却至关重要的一环。

By the end of this chapter, you'll have a practical framework for growing into the role of a tech lead and strategies for navigating the challenges that come with it.

读完本章，你将获得一套可落地的框架，用来成长为技术负责人，并掌握应对随之而来的各种挑战的策略。

Setting the Foundation for Growth为成长打好基础

Before you can grow with intention, you need a solid foundation. That starts with how you think, what you understand about your role, and where you currently stand.

在你能够有意识地成长之前，需要先有一个坚实的基础。这始于你的思维方式、你对自身角色的理解，以及你目前所处的位置。

— PDF p.50 —

It begins with mindset. Embracing a growth mindset means seeing challenges as opportunities to improve and understanding that mistakes are part of the learning process, not something to fear or avoid.

一切始于心态。拥抱成长型思维，意味着把挑战视为提升的机会，并明白错误是学习过程的一部分，而不是需要害怕或回避的东西。

But mindset alone isn't enough. You also need clarity. What's expected of you? What does success look like in your team, your company, your context? By talking with your manager, your stakeholders, and even your peers, you can start to shape a more realistic and grounded picture of what to aim for.

但光有心态还不够。你还需要清晰。公司对你的期望是什么？在你的团队、你的公司、你的具体处境中，成功长什么样？通过与经理、利益相关者甚至同事交流，你可以逐步勾勒出一幅更现实、更扎实的画面，明确自己该朝什么方向努力。

And once that picture is clearer, you can take a good, honest look at where you're starting from. What are your strengths? Where are your gaps? This kind of self-assessment isn't always easy, but it's essential if you want to grow with purpose rather than just reacting to whatever comes next.

一旦这幅画面变得清晰，你就可以坦诚地审视自己的起点在哪里。你的优势是什么？差距又在哪里？这种自我评估并不总是容易的，但如果你想有目标地成长、而不是被动应付接踵而来的事情，它就必不可少。

These early steps, including how you think, what you understand, and how you reflect, will shape everything that follows. Let's get into it.

这些早期步骤——包括你的思维方式、你的理解、你的反思——将塑造此后的一切。我们这就开始。

Build a Growth Mindset建立成长型思维

Having a growth plan is effective only if you pair it with the right mindset. To grow as a tech lead, you need to embrace a growth mindset, which is the belief that your abilities can be developed through effort, learning, and perseverance. It's about seeing challenges as opportunities and mistakes as learning experiences, rather than failures.

成长计划只有配上正确的心态才能奏效。要成长为技术负责人，你需要拥抱成长型思维——即相信自己的能力可以通过努力、学习和坚持来发展。它意味着把挑战视为机会，把错误视为学习经历，而非失败。

When I first stepped into the tech lead role, I believed I had to have all the answers and get everything right. I felt like every mistake or moment of uncertainty would undermine my capability in the eyes of others. I would hide my mistakes, thinking it made me appear more competent. I'd prepare technical solutions in advance, rushing to respond to every client question as if hesitation would make me seem less qualified. My anxiety drove me to over-prepare for every situation, leaving me constantly stressed and exhausted.

我刚走上技术负责人岗位时，以为自己必须掌握所有答案、把每件事都做对。我觉得每一个错误、每一刻的不确定，都会在别人眼里削弱我的能力。我会掩盖自己的错误，以为这样会显得自己更能干。我会提前准备好技术方案，急着回应客户的每一个问题，仿佛一旦迟疑就会显得我不够格。我的焦虑驱使我为每种状况过度准备，结果长期压力山大、疲惫不堪。

When others didn't have answers, I felt it was my responsibility to step in and “fix it all,” often taking on tasks that weren't mine to handle. Instead of asking for clarification, I'd spend hours figuring things out alone, convinced that admitting I didn't know something would damage my credibility.

当别人答不上来时，我觉得自己有责任站出来“把一切搞定”，常常揽下本不该由我处理的任务。我不去寻求澄清，而是独自花上好几个小时琢磨，因为我坚信承认自己不懂会损害我的可信度。

Looking back, I realize how limiting this mindset was, because growth requires a fundamental belief: you don't need to have all the answers right away, but you do need to believe in your ability to learn, adapt, and improve:

回头看，我才意识到这种心态有多局限，因为成长需要一个根本性的信念：你不需要立刻拥有所有答案，但你必须相信自己有能力去学习、适应和提升。

In order to grow, you need to believe you need to.

想要成长，你首先得相信自己需要成长。

— PDF p.51 —

The good news is, a growth mindset can be developed just like any other skill. Two strategies helped me transform my approach to challenges and uncertainty.

好消息是，成长型思维和其他任何技能一样是可以后天培养的。有两个策略帮我彻底改变了面对挑战与不确定性的方式。

The first is embracing the phrase “I don't know.” Admitting when you don't have all the answers can be a game-changer. It allows you to learn faster by seeking information instead of pretending, reduces the stress of trying to appear all-knowing, and supports a culture of collaboration by making it safe for others to admit what they don't know as well. At first, saying “I don't know” felt uncomfortable; I even got strange looks from others. But over time, it became easier, and I began to see how it strengthened my interactions and trust within the team.

第一个策略是坦然说出“我不知道”。承认自己并非无所不知，会成为一个转折点。它让你通过主动寻求信息——而不是不懂装懂——来学得更快；它减轻了那种必须显得全知全能的压力；它还能促进协作文化，因为这让别人也敢于承认自己不懂。起初，说“我不知道”让我浑身不自在，甚至招来异样的目光。但久而久之，这变得容易了，我也开始看到它如何加强了我与团队的互动和信任。

I know this can feel intimidating, and in some environments, even more so. It's especially tough in client-facing situations or in cultures where vulnerability might be viewed as a weakness. I still remember the first time I said “I don't know” in front of a client. It felt ten times harder than saying it to my team. But over time, I saw the same positive effect: it created space for honesty and showed that not knowing is normal. Eventually, more people began to follow. Someone has to be the first to have the courage to say it out loud.

我知道这会让人胆怯，在某些环境下更是如此。在面对客户的场合，或是在那种“展露脆弱会被视为软弱”的文化里，尤其难。我还记得第一次在客户面前说“我不知道”，那感觉比对团队说要难上十倍。但久而久之，我看到了同样的积极效果：它为坦诚创造了空间，也表明“不知道”是再正常不过的事。最终，越来越多的人开始效仿。总得有人第一个鼓起勇气把它大声说出来。

The second strategy is shifting from “I don't know” to “I don't know yet.” Reflecting on past challenges often reveals a pattern: you didn't always know the answers, but you figured them out. Think back to moments when you started and you lacked clarity or certainty. What steps did you take to move forward? How did you overcome the fear of not succeeding? Over time, what initially felt impossible became second nature. This mindset shift focuses on the journey of learning and emphasizes that progress takes time and effort.

第二个策略，是把“我不知道”转变成“我现在还不知道”。回顾过去遇到的挑战，往往会发现一个规律：你并非一开始就知道答案，但你最终把它弄明白了。回想一下你刚起步、前路模糊或心中没底的那些时刻。你采取了哪些步骤往前走？你是如何克服“怕做不成”的恐惧的？久而久之，最初觉得不可能的事变成了你的第二天性。这种心态转变聚焦于学习的旅程，并强调进步需要时间和努力。

When it comes to growth, it's also helpful to remember that confidence doesn't always reflect competence. The Dunning-Kruger effect describes how people with limited experience tend to overestimate their abilities, while those who are more skilled often underestimate themselves. If you're doubting your abilities, it might actually be a sign that you're becoming more aware of what mastery really involves, which is a key step in growing. See Figure 2-1 for a visual of the Dunning-Kruger curve, which illustrates how confidence often dips as awareness increases before rising again with true competence.

说到成长，还有一点很值得记住：自信并不总能反映能力。邓宁-克鲁格效应（Dunning-Kruger effect）描述的是：经验有限的人往往高估自己的能力，而真正更有本事的人却常常低估自己。如果你正在怀疑自己的能力，这其实可能恰恰说明你越来越清楚“精通”究竟意味着什么——而这正是成长中的关键一步。图 2-1 展示了邓宁-克鲁格曲线，它说明：随着认知加深，信心往往会先下跌，然后才随着真正能力的提升而回升。

— PDF p.52 —

It's easy to feel the pressure to know everything, but real growth happens when you trust your ability to learn and adapt. Confidence doesn't come from always having the answers; it comes from recognizing what you know now and believing you'll figure out the rest. Growth starts with this belief. You won't know everything right away, but with time and effort, you will.

人很容易感到“必须无所不知”的压力，但真正的成长发生在你相信自己有能力学习和适应的时候。自信并非来自永远手握答案，而是来自认清你现在已知的部分，并相信其余的你迟早能弄明白。成长始于这份信念。你不会一下子就什么都懂，但只要时间和精力到位，你终将做到。

Tip: For a deeper exploration of the growth mindset, I highly recommend Mindset: The New Psychology of Success by Carol Dweck (Random House).

提示：如需深入探究成长型思维，我强烈推荐 Carol Dweck 的《Mindset: The New Psychology of Success》（Random House 出版）。

Clarify Expectations厘清期望

The second requirement for growth is understanding what's expected of you. The tech lead role can vary widely between companies, so it's important to clarify expectations in your specific environment.

成长的第二个前提，是弄清楚别人对你的期望。技术负责人这个角色在不同公司之间差异很大，因此在你所处的具体环境中厘清期望非常重要。

One of the most common surprises I hear in coaching is from tech leads who thought they were expected to focus on technical delivery, only to later realize their manager cared more about team development and cross-functional collaboration.

在辅导中，我最常听到的“意外”之一是：一些技术负责人原以为公司期望他们专注于技术交付，结果后来才意识到，经理更关心的是团队发展和跨职能协作。

— PDF p.53 —

For example, one coaching client stepped into a tech lead role assuming she needed to drive architectural decisions and write the hardest parts of the code. But after a few months, she received feedback that she wasn't visible enough to the team and wasn't spending enough time on mentoring or stakeholder communication.

举个例子，有位辅导对象刚上任技术负责人时，以为自己要主导架构决策、亲手写最难的那部分代码。但几个月后，她收到的反馈却是：她在团队面前的存在感不够，也没有花足够时间做辅导和利益相关者沟通。

This situation could have been avoided by clarifying expectations early on. The section “Understanding the Expectations of Your Role” on page 12 offers practical strategies to help you do just that, so you can align your efforts with what your organization actually values from the start.

这种局面本可以通过尽早厘清期望来避免。第 12 页“理解你角色的期望”一节提供了实用策略，帮你做到这一点，让你从一开始就把精力投向组织真正看重的地方。

With these expectations in mind, the next step is to figure out where you stand in relation to them.

心中有了这些期望，下一步就是对照它们，弄清楚自己目前所处的位置。

Assess Your Starting Point评估你的起点

Once you've clarified the expectations for your role, you can use them to get a clearer picture of where you stand right now. They provide a concrete reference point to define your baseline. A simple way to do this is by using a 1-to-10 scaling system (where 1 means “just starting out” and 10 means “strong in this area”), shown in Table 2-1.

一旦你厘清了对角色的期望，就可以用它们来更清晰地看清自己现在所处的位置。它们提供了一个具体的参照点，用来定义你的基线。一个简单的做法是使用 1 到 10 的评分体系（1 表示“刚刚起步”，10 表示“在这方面很强”），如表 2-1 所示。

Step步骤Description说明Reflection Prompt反思提示
Rate yourself给自己打分Review the expectations identified in the previous section, “Clarify Expectations” on page 36. Rate yourself from 1 to 10 for each area. Use examples. Pay attention not just to what's missing but also to what you're already strong at.回顾上一节（第 36 页“厘清期望”）中确定的各项期望。针对每个方面给自己打 1 到 10 分，并举例说明。不仅要关注自己欠缺什么，也要留意你已经擅长什么。Why this rating? Why not a 10? What's missing to get to a 10?为什么打这个分？为什么不是 10 分？要达到 10 分还差什么？
Seek feedback寻求反馈Ask colleagues and your manager to rate you on the same scale. Request specific examples to support their rating and suggestions for improvement.请同事和经理用同一把尺子给你打分。请他们给出具体例子来支撑评分，并提出改进建议。What am I already doing well in this area? What's one thing I could do to improve this area?在这个方面，我已经做得不错的是什么？我能做的一件改进是什么？
Compare and align对比并校准Look at how your self-ratings compare to the feedback. Identify gaps and strengths to inform your growth plan.看看你的自评与他人反馈之间有何差异。找出差距和优势，作为你成长计划的依据。Where are the biggest gaps? What surprised you?最大的差距在哪里？有什么让你意外的发现？
— PDF p.54 —

The main reason why I like this framework is that it forces people to actually evaluate where they are. It's not about the number but about the reflection it triggers. In my experience, people tend to undervalue themselves when self-rating. Many of my coaching clients say things like “I could never rate myself a 10; that just feels like bragging,” even when they can't identify a single improvement point in that area. You have to consider that if nothing's missing, maybe you're already a 10.

我之所以喜欢这个框架，主要原因在于它迫使人们真正去评估自己所处的位置。重点不在那个数字，而在它触发的反思。以我的经验，人们在自我评价时往往会低估自己。我的许多辅导对象会说类似“我绝对不可能给自己打 10 分，那感觉就像在吹牛”这样的话——哪怕他们在那个领域已经找不出任何一点可以改进的地方。你得这样想：如果真的什么都不缺，那也许你本来就已经是 10 分了。

It's a shame to automatically downgrade yourself like that. If you don't stand up for yourself, who will? Let others point out the gaps. Your job is to own your strengths with clarity and confidence.

像这样自动给自己降格，实在可惜。如果你不为自己站出来，还会有谁呢？让别人去指出你的差距吧。你的任务，是清晰而自信地认领自己的长处。

Developing a Personal Growth Plan制定个人成长计划

People often get trapped in the cycle of “doing” without a clear destination, which can drain motivation. I've been there, focusing on tasks without knowing exactly where they're leading. A growth plan changes that by being intentional about where you want to go. It gives you control over your career path, helping you recognize opportunities as they come and make decisions more easily because you know your “why.” It's about moving with purpose rather than drifting on someone else's agenda.

人们常常陷入“一味做事”却没有明确目标的循环，这会消耗动力。我也经历过：埋头于各种任务，却不知道它们究竟把我带向何方。成长计划改变了这一点——它让你有意识地决定自己想去哪里。它让你掌握自己职业道路的主动权，帮助你在机会出现时认出它，并因为你清楚自己的“为什么”而更容易做决策。它关乎带着目标前行，而不是随波逐流、围着别人的日程转。

The five steps for building a growth plan are as follows.

制定成长计划分为以下五个步骤。

Step 1: Define a Clear Goal第一步：定义一个清晰的目标

A lot of people struggle to define meaningful career goals, especially when transitioning from individual contributor to leadership roles. It's not always easy to articulate what you want beyond a title like “tech lead.” That's why it helps to go deeper and get specific.

很多人都难以定义有意义的职业目标，尤其是在从个人贡献者转型到领导岗位时。要说清楚除了“技术负责人”这个头衔之外你到底想要什么，并不总是容易。所以，往深处挖、说得越具体越有帮助。

Ask yourself the following questions:

问问自己以下几个问题：

  • What would success look like in this role?在这个岗位上，成功会是什么样子？
  • How will I know I've reached my goal?我要怎么知道自己已经达成了目标？
  • What will be different in my day-to-day work?我的日常工作会有什么不同？

But don't stop there. One of the most important questions I ask people when they're seeking a promotion is this: Why do you want it? Is it about recognition, influence, salary, visibility, or something else? Most people's answers are different, and knowing yours can help ensure the goal is truly aligned with your deeper motivation. Sometimes, the promotion you're chasing isn't the only (or best) way to get what you're after.

但不要就此打住。当人们寻求晋升时，我问的最重要的问题之一是：你为什么想要它？是为了认可、影响力、薪水、曝光度，还是别的什么？大多数人的答案各不相同，而弄清你自己的答案，能帮你确保这个目标真正与你更深层的动机相一致。有时候，你苦苦追求的晋升，并不是获得你所想要之物的唯一（甚至也不是最好的）途径。

— PDF p.55 —

So instead of just saying, “I want to become a tech lead,” try defining what that means to you:

所以，不要只说“我想成为技术负责人”，试着把它对你而言具体意味着什么定义出来：

  • Leading a team of five engineers on a customer-facing product在一个面向客户的产品上带领一支五人工程师团队
  • Taking over the tech lead role in my current team when my tech lead leaves当我现在的技术负责人离职时，接手我所在团队的技术负责人角色
  • Having the official tech lead title拿到正式的技术负责人头衔

The more specific you are, the easier it is to use this goal.

你定义得越具体，这个目标就越容易被利用起来。

Tip: If you're unsure, look at job descriptions or company expectations, or talk to current tech leads. Ask them: “What made you feel like you were finally in the role?”

提示：如果你不确定，可以看看职位描述或公司的期望，或者找现任技术负责人聊聊。问他们：“是什么让你觉得自己终于真正胜任这个角色了？”

Step 2: Define the Steps to Get There第二步：定义通往目标的步骤

Once you've defined your goal, the next challenge is turning it into action. This is where many people get stuck: they know what they want but aren't sure how to start moving toward it.

一旦你定义好了目标，下一个挑战就是把它转化为行动。很多人就卡在这里：他们知道自己想要什么，却不确定该如何朝它迈出第一步。

Break the goal into milestones: think of them as checkpoints on the path to your destination. These are not just tasks but progress markers that show you're moving in the right direction.

把目标拆成若干里程碑：把它们想象成通往目的地道路上的一个个检查点。它们不只是任务，更是进度标志，标示着你正在朝正确的方向前进。

Ask yourself the following questions:

问问自己以下几个问题：

  • What needs to be true for me to reach this goal?要达成这个目标，哪些条件必须成立？
  • What skills or experiences am I currently missing?我目前还欠缺哪些技能或经验？
  • What small steps can I take in the next week or month?在接下来的一周或一个月里，我能迈出哪些小步？

If the path feels fuzzy, back into it by identifying one or two immediate opportunities already available to you. You don't need a full roadmap, just enough clarity to start walking. You can figure out steps along the way also.

如果这条路感觉模糊不清，那就反过来做：先找出一两个你眼下就能抓住的机会。你不需要一张完整的路线图，只需要足够清晰、能迈出第一步就行。剩下的步骤，你完全可以边走边琢磨。

Tip: Review past feedback or performance reviews. Often, they contain useful clues about what you could be doing more of or be doing differently.

提示：回顾过去的反馈或绩效评估。它们往往藏着有用的线索，告诉你哪些事可以多做、哪些事可以换种做法。

— PDF p.56 —

Step 3: Build a Timeline第三步：搭建时间线

Now that you have a goal and a set of steps, it's time to add some structure. A timeline gives your plan momentum. It turns vague intentions into commitments and helps you hold yourself accountable.

现在你有了目标和一组步骤，是时候加上一些结构了。时间线能给你的计划注入动力。它把模糊的意愿变成承诺，并帮你对自己负责。

This doesn't mean everything has to be perfectly scheduled. The idea is to set rough timeframes for each step or milestone so you can track progress and avoid stalling out.

这并不意味着每件事都必须安排得严丝合缝。关键是为每个步骤或里程碑设定大致的时间框架，好让你能跟踪进度、避免停滞不前。

Ask yourself the following:

问问自己以下问题：

  • What can I realistically work on this quarter?这个季度我现实地能推进些什么？
  • Are there natural checkpoints I can use, like a performance review, team change, or project cycle?有没有一些现成的检查点可以利用，比如一次绩效评估、一次团队变动，或一个项目周期？
  • Which steps depend on others, and how long might those take?哪些步骤依赖他人？那些事大概要花多久？

Use a calendar, spreadsheet, or project board (like Trello or Notion) to map it out visually. Seeing it laid out can make the plan feel more real and manageable.

用日历、电子表格或项目看板（比如 Trello 或 Notion）把它可视化地排出来。看着它被铺开，会让计划感觉更真实、更可把握。

Tip: If you're unsure about timelines, start with short-term goals and adjust as you learn more. Even a rough guess is better than none; it gives you a direction and makes it easier to reflect and improve later.

提示：如果你对时间线没把握，就先从短期目标开始，随着了解加深再调整。哪怕只是一个粗略的猜测，也比没有强；它给你一个方向，也让你之后更容易复盘和改进。

Step 4: Build a Support Network第四步：搭建支持网络

One of the most overlooked, but powerful, parts of a growth plan is asking, “Who can help me?”

成长计划中最被忽视、却又最有力量的一环，是问自己一句：“谁能帮我？”

Growth doesn't happen in isolation. The people around you—your manager, your current tech lead, mentors, peers, or even a coach—can play a huge role in how fast and smoothly you progress.

成长不会在真空中发生。你身边的人——你的经理、你现在的技术负责人、导师、同事，甚至一位教练——都能对你进步的速度与顺畅程度起到巨大作用。

Different people can support you in different ways: your manager can give visibility into future opportunities, suggest growth areas, and connect your goals to team needs; your current tech lead might let you shadow them or gradually take over rituals like planning or standups; mentors or peers can share how they approached similar transitions and offer perspective from outside your team; a coach can help you reflect, challenge your assumptions, and stay focused.

不同的人能以不同方式支持你：你的经理可以让你看到未来的机会、指出可以成长的领域，并把你的目标与团队需求对接起来；你现在的技术负责人可能会让你跟着他观摩，或逐步接手规划、站会这类例行事务；导师或同事可以分享他们是如何应对类似转型的，并提供来自团队之外的视角；教练则可以帮你复盘、挑战你的固有假设，并让你保持专注。

— PDF p.57 —

Let them in on your goals. When people know what you're aiming for, they can offer better feedback, suggest relevant opportunities, or support you when you need a push. Be proactive: ask for a regular check-in, share updates on your progress, and ask for help identifying blind spots.

让他们知道你的目标。当人们清楚你想奔向哪里时，他们才能给出更好的反馈、推荐相关的机会，或在你需要推一把的时候支持你。要主动：请求定期一对一交流、分享你的进展更新、并请他们帮你指出盲区。

This isn't about asking people to “do it for you” but about building a circle of support that helps you grow faster and more sustainably.

这不是要请别人“替你去做”，而是要构建一个支持圈，帮你更快、更可持续地成长。

Step 5: Identify Opportunities and Resources第五步：识别机会与资源

A solid plan also takes advantage of what's already around you. The question here is “What opportunities and resources can I tap into to help me grow?”

一份扎实的计划还会善用你身边已经存在的东西。这里要问的问题是：“我能借助哪些机会和资源来帮助自己成长？”

Start with your current role. There are likely more learning opportunities than you realize; you just need to spot them or ask for them. Look for growth moments like leading a team retrospective, even if informally; taking the lead on a small project or feature; facilitating technical discussions; mentoring a more junior team member; or owning a process improvement (like refining your team's release workflow).

从你当前的角色开始。身边的学习机会很可能比你意识到的更多，你只需要发现它们，或者主动去要。留意这样的成长时刻：主持一次团队复盘（哪怕是非正式的）；牵头一个小项目或一个小功能；主持技术讨论；带一位更初级的团队成员；或主导一次流程改进（比如优化你团队的发布流程）。

Ask your manager or tech lead, “Is there an area where I could take more ownership or help the team?” You'd be surprised how often the answer is yes.

问问你的经理或技术负责人：“有没有哪个方面我可以承担更多责任、或帮团队一把？”你会惊讶地发现，答案常常是肯定的。

Next, look outside your day-to-day tasks: shadowing others (e.g., sitting in on planning meetings, architecture reviews), contributing to cross-team initiatives or guilds, presenting at internal knowledge-sharing sessions, or writing technical documentation or proposals.

接下来，把目光放到日常任务之外：观摩别人（比如列席规划会议、架构评审）；参与跨团队的项目或技术社群（guild）；在内部知识分享会上做演讲；或撰写技术文档、技术提案。

And don't forget about formal resources, like your learning and development (L&D) budget. Use them for leadership courses, workshops, coaching, books, podcasts, communities, internal or external leadership programs, or training opportunities.

也别忘了正式的资源，比如你的学习与发展（L&D）预算。把它用在领导力课程、工作坊、教练辅导、书籍、播客、社区、内部或外部领导力项目，以及各类培训机会上。

To make this more tangible, let's walk through how these five steps come together in practice. The example in Table 2-2 outlines a growth plan for someone aiming to take over the tech lead role in their current team when their tech lead leaves.

为了让这一切更具体，我们来看看这五个步骤在实践中是如何组合到一起的。表 2-2 给出了一份成长计划示例：主角的目标是在自己团队的技术负责人离职后，接手该团队的技术负责人岗位。

— PDF p.58 —
Step步骤Example示例
Define a clear goal定义清晰目标Become the tech lead of my current team成为我当前团队的技术负责人
Define the steps to get there定义通往目标的步骤Inform current tech lead and manager about my intention; shadow current tech lead during strategy planning; lead the migration initiative in the team告知现任技术负责人和经理我的意向；在战略规划期间跟随现任技术负责人观摩；在团队中牵头迁移项目
Build a timeline搭建时间线Timeline from Feb to Jul: lead the migration initiative in the team; shadow current tech lead during strategy planning (see figure below)时间线从二月到七月：期间在团队中牵头迁移项目；并在战略规划期间跟随现任技术负责人观摩（见下图）
Build a support network搭建支持网络Schedule one-on-ones with manager; ask Ana (a tech lead from another team) to be my mentor; join the monthly company “tech lead conversations”与经理安排一对一沟通；请 Ana（来自另一个团队的技术负责人）做我的导师；参加公司每月一次的“技术负责人对话”
Identify opportunities and resources识别机会与资源Use L&D budget for leadership course (be specific); read Leveling Up as a Tech Lead; take the Soft Skills for Tech Leads O'Reilly online course; read The Manager's Path by Camille Fournier; join the LeadDev community用 L&D 预算上领导力课程（要具体）；阅读《Leveling Up as a Tech Lead》；参加 O'Reilly 在线课程《Soft Skills for Tech Leads》；阅读 Camille Fournier 的《The Manager's Path》；加入 LeadDev 社区

The plan may not always go as expected, but it will get you to your goal faster than just going with the flow. Keep adjusting as you progress.

计划未必总能按预想推进，但它会比随波逐流更快地把你送到目标。随着推进持续调整就好。

Implementing the Growth Plan执行成长计划

This is the part where your growth plan comes to life.

到了这一步，你的成长计划开始真正落地。

You've defined your big goals; now it's time to put them aside for a moment and start zooming in. Focus on the small, concrete steps you outlined in your growth plan. Start acting on them one by one while constantly reflecting on what's working and what isn't.

你已经定义好了大目标；现在是时候把它们先放一放，开始拉近镜头、聚焦细节。专注于你在成长计划里列出的那些具体小步骤。一条一条地开始行动，同时不断反思哪些有效、哪些无效。

Reflect复盘

Reflection is a tool that vastly accelerates your growth. For each step you take, assess whether you're aligned with your growth plan. Ask yourself, “Am I making progress?” and “What adjustments are necessary?” Use your milestones as checkpoints to assess whether your actions still support your bigger direction.

复盘是一个能极大加速你成长的工具。每采取一个步骤，都评估一下自己是否与成长计划保持一致。问问自己：“我有在进步吗？”“需要做哪些调整？”把你的里程碑当作检查点，用来评估你的行动是否仍然支撑着你更大的方向。

— PDF p.59 —

A simple way to evaluate your progress is to repeat the same 1-to-10 scaling system described in the section “Assess Your Starting Point” on page 37. Revisit your ratings, ask for updated feedback from others, and have recurring conversations with your team, manager, or peers about your development. These insights can validate your progress or surface areas that need more attention.

一个评估进展的简单办法，是重做第 37 页“评估你的起点”一节里那套 1 到 10 的评分体系。重新审视你的评分，请别人给出更新后的反馈，并定期与你的团队、经理或同事聊聊你的成长。这些洞见既能验证你的进展，也能暴露出需要更多关注的地方。

Getting honest, useful feedback is harder than it seems. People might hesitate to be direct, especially when you're in a position of authority. That's why it's important to create psychological safety, ask thoughtful questions, and normalize feedback as a regular part of working together. Chapter 5 includes the section “How to Get Useful Feedback from Your Team”, which dives into specific strategies you can use to gather meaningful input from both team members and stakeholders.

获得诚实而有用的反馈，比看上去要难。人们可能会犹豫要不要直说，尤其是当你身处权威位置时。因此，营造心理安全感、提出有深度的问题、并把反馈变成协作中稀松平常的一部分，就显得尤为重要。第 5 章中有一节“如何从你的团队获得有用的反馈”，深入介绍了具体策略，帮你从团队成员和利益相关者那里收集有意义的意见。

Track Your Progress跟踪你的进展

Whatever comes up at each reflection point, track it. It sounds so simple, but this critical step is often dismissed as “obvious” and skipped entirely. The result? You lose sight of how far you've come and the progress you've made.

每到一个复盘点，无论浮现出什么，都把它记录下来。这听上去简单得不能再简单，但这个关键步骤却常常被当成“理所当然”而直接跳过。结果呢？你会忘记自己已经走了多远、取得了多少进展。

You can track your progress in whatever format works best for you. Some people prefer a handwritten journal or notebook, while others use a spreadsheet, a Notion page, or a digital app like Trello or Todoist. The key is to make your progress visible. A simple table with your goals, key steps, timeline, and a column for status/notes or reflections (like in Table 2-3) can go a long way.

你可以用任何最适合你的方式来跟踪进展。有人喜欢手写日记或笔记本，有人用电子表格、Notion 页面，或 Trello、Todoist 这类数字应用。关键是让你的进展变得可见。一张简单的表格，列上你的目标、关键步骤、时间线，再加一列状态/备注或反思（如表 2-3 所示），就能发挥很大作用。

Goal目标Step步骤Timeline时间线Status/Notes状态/备注
Improve collaboration in the team改善团队协作Pair program with three different team members与三位不同的团队成员结对编程By August 1st8 月 1 日前June 3rd: paired with one team member6 月 3 日：已与一位团队成员结对
Improve collaboration in the team改善团队协作Have two other team members pair together on a task让另外两位团队成员在一项任务上结对By August 1st8 月 1 日前June 3rd: the plan is for them to pair next week6 月 3 日：计划安排他们下周结对
Improve collaboration in the team改善团队协作Have two team knowledge-sharing sessions举办两次团队知识分享会By August 1st8 月 1 日前June 15th: I delivered the first session; encouraged another team member to lead next6 月 15 日：我主持了第一场；已鼓励另一位团队成员主持下一场
— PDF p.60 —

You can be as specific as you like or keep it extremely lightweight. In fact, the simpler your system, the more likely you are to stick with it. It could be as easy as keeping a running list in a notes app where you jot down small wins as they happen. For example: “June 3rd: Convinced Alex to pair with me on the new onboarding flow, and it went really smoothly.” You can later match these small wins to the goals you've defined for yourself, which is especially useful during performance review cycles, where clear, goal-aligned examples go a long way.

你可以想多具体就多具体，也可以把它做得极其轻量。事实上，你的系统越简单，你就越有可能坚持下来。简单到什么程度呢？可以就在一个笔记应用里维护一个滚动清单，随手记下一个个小小的胜利。比如：“6 月 3 日：说服了 Alex 和我一起结对做新的 onboarding 流程，过程非常顺利。”之后你可以把这些小胜利对应到你为自己设定的目标上——这在绩效评估周期里尤其有用，因为清晰、与目标对齐的例子非常有说服力。

Many people avoid tracking progress for reasons that might seem valid at first.

很多人会因为一些乍听之下挺有道理的理由，而回避记录进展。

Some feel that being structured about their growth is selfish or self-centered, something others might frown upon. I constantly have to remind people that there's nothing wrong with wanting to grow and become a better person or professional.

有些人觉得，对自己的成长搞得这么有规划，是自私、以自我为中心，别人可能会不喜欢。我得不断提醒人们：想要成长、想成为更好的人或更专业的人，这一点错都没有。

Others hesitate, asking, “What counts as progress?” The answer is straightforward: anything, big or small, that moves you forward is worth recording.

还有些人会犹豫，问：“到底什么才算进展？”答案很直接：任何让你向前的事，无论大小，都值得记录。

Then there's the classic excuse: “I'll remember it.” The reality is, you probably won't, just like many tech leads I talk to daily. And why overburden your brain when writing things down is far easier and more effective? Writing things down activates a different part of your brain, making your progress feel tangible and keeping you connected to the steps you've taken. These small habits, simple as they may seem, can fundamentally shift how you perceive and maintain your growth.

然后还有那个经典的借口：“我会记住的。”现实是，你大概率记不住——就像我每天聊到的许多技术负责人一样。既然写下来要容易得多、也有效得多，又何必让大脑超负荷运转呢？写下来会激活你大脑的另一个区域，让你的进展变得可感知，并把你与自己迈出的每一步连在一起。这些小习惯看似简单，却能从根本上改变你看待和维系自身成长的方式。

You don't need to track daily, but finding a regular rhythm that works for you, whether it's weekly, biweekly, or monthly, can make a big difference. The key is consistency.

你不需要每天都记录，但找到一个适合自己的固定节奏——不管是每周、每两周还是每月——都会大有不同。关键在于坚持。

Tracking offers two significant benefits. First, it boosts your self-confidence. On tough days, looking back at the challenges you've overcome reminds you of how capable you are. Second, it provides motivation. Progress can feel painfully slow when you're focused only on the long road ahead, but reflecting on how far you've come can restart your drive to keep going.

记录能带来两个重要的好处。第一，它提升你的自信。在艰难的日子里，回头看看你已经克服的那些挑战，会提醒你自己有多能干。第二，它提供动力。当你只盯着前方漫漫长路时，进展会慢得让人难受；但回顾你已经走了多远，能重新点燃你继续前行的动力。

Tip: Don't skip reflection. It helps you stay motivated and on track.

提示：不要跳过复盘。它能帮你保持动力、不偏离轨道。

Adjust调整

Growth isn't static; it's a continuous process of learning and adapting. Use the feedback and insights you've gathered to refine your next steps.

成长不是静止的；它是一个不断学习、不断适应的过程。用你收集到的反馈和洞见，去打磨你的下一步。

Start by being intentional about what you focus on next. If you want to work on your communication skills, lean into people interaction and find opportunities to practice. If there's a technical area you want to deepen your knowledge in, prioritize pairing with experienced team members and working on tasks that stretch you. This is how you take control over your growth instead of just going with the flow.

首先，要有意识地决定下一步聚焦什么。如果你想提升沟通能力，就多扎进与人打交道的场合，找机会练习。如果你想在某个技术领域加深知识，就优先和有经验的团队成员结对、去做那些能拉伸你能力的任务。这才是主动掌控自己的成长，而不是随波逐流。

— PDF p.61 —

Be strategic about your environment. If you can choose your projects, pick ones that help diversify your experience. But even within your current role, there are plenty of opportunities to grow; you just have to be intentional about spotting them.

要有策略地选择你所处的环境。如果可以选择项目，就选那些能丰富你经验广度的。但即便在你现有的角色里，也有大把成长机会；你只需要有意识地去发现它们。

By implementing, reflecting, tracking progress, and adjusting, you'll turn your growth plan into a dynamic tool that evolves with your goals and context, keeping you on track to becoming an effective tech lead.

通过执行、复盘、跟踪进展和调整，你会把成长计划变成一个动态工具，随你的目标和处境不断演进，让你始终走在成为一名高效技术负责人的轨道上。

Overcoming Common Initial Challenges应对初期常见的挑战

When I talk to tech leads, I see the same struggles coming up time and time again. Some feel overwhelmed trying to manage their time effectively and balance their focus among technical responsibilities, team dynamics, and stakeholder needs. Others fall into the trap of trying to solve everyone's problems or micromanaging their team. These challenges are not just common; they're expected. But they don't have to derail you.

当我和技术负责人聊天时，会看到同样的困境一次又一次地出现。有些人被压得喘不过气：既要有效管理时间，又要在技术职责、团队动态和利益相关者需求之间分配精力。另一些人则掉进了“想解决所有人问题”或“对团队微观管理”的陷阱。这些挑战不仅常见，而且是意料之中的。但它们未必能把你带偏。

In the sections that follow, I'll walk you through these recurring challenges one by one and share strategies for navigating them effectively, starting with time management.

在接下来的几节里，我会一个一个地带你走过这些反复出现的挑战，并分享有效应对它们的策略——先从时间管理开始。

Time Management时间管理

In the section “Day-to-day Responsibilities” on page 10, I outlined the core daily tasks for a tech lead: meetings, coding, and thinking time. However, no matter how well you plan, disruptions are inevitable, whether it's production incidents, strategy changes, or team conflicts. You need to be prepared to switch lanes and adapt.

在第 10 页“日常职责”一节中，我列出了技术负责人每天的核心任务：会议、写代码和思考时间。然而，无论你计划得多好，干扰都不可避免——无论是生产事故、战略变动，还是团队冲突。你需要做好切换车道、随机应变的准备。

While flexibility is key, it's still important to have a time management system in place. Time management is a major challenge for most tech leads, and this section will help you build a process to gain control over your time and handle disruptions effectively.

虽然灵活性很关键，但建立一套时间管理体系仍然重要。时间管理对大多数技术负责人来说都是一大挑战，本节会帮你搭建一套流程，让你重新掌控自己的时间，并有效应对干扰。

— PDF p.62 —

Step 1: Visualize your workload第一步：可视化你的工作负荷

Visualizing your workload can help you spot priorities, manage your time more effectively, and reduce overwhelm. There are many ways to do this, and different formats work better for different people.

把工作负荷可视化，能帮你发现优先级、更有效地管理时间，并减轻被压垮的感觉。做法有很多种，不同的形式适合不同的人。

You might prefer using a color-coded task list to quickly flag urgent and non-urgent work. Mind maps can help you see how tasks relate to each other and to broader goals. Kanban boards (physical or digital) are great for visualizing progress and balancing workload. Some people use weekly planning templates or calendar blocking to map time against task types.

你可能更喜欢用一张带颜色标记的任务清单，快速标出紧急和不紧急的工作。思维导图能帮你看清任务之间、以及任务与更大目标之间的关系。看板（实体的或电子的）非常适合可视化进度、平衡工作量。有些人用每周计划模板或日历时间块，把时间对应到不同类型的任务上。

There's no one best method; it's about what helps you stay focused and intentional.

没有唯一最好的方法；关键是哪种能帮你保持专注和有意识。

As an example, I'm using the Eisenhower Matrix here to show you how one approach can help you sort tasks by urgency and importance. In Figure 2-2, you'll find examples of what types of tasks fit into each quadrant.

举个例子，我这里用艾森豪威尔矩阵（Eisenhower Matrix）来演示，这套方法如何帮你按紧急程度和重要性对任务分类。在图 2-2 中，你会看到每种类型的任务分别落在哪个象限。

Let's take a practical example: a typical first attempt by a tech lead to populate the Eisenhower Matrix, as shown in Figure 2-3.

来看一个实际例子：如图 2-3 所示，这是一位技术负责人第一次尝试填写艾森豪威尔矩阵时的典型样子。

— PDF p.63 —

Step 2: Analyze your task distribution and adjust your workload第二步：分析任务分布并调整工作负荷

When you look at your task list, there are a few things to keep in mind. First, take a moment to step back and ask yourself: do you have tasks in all four quadrants? One of the most common struggles for tech leads during this exercise is that they fill in only the top two quadrants, as you can see in Figure 2-3. When asked why, the answer is almost always the same: “Everything is important; that's why it's on my list.” This is a classic example of the urgency effect, a cognitive bias where we tend to prioritize tasks that appear urgent, often at the expense of more important but less time-sensitive work. Just because something feels immediate doesn't mean it deserves your time or energy.

当你审视自己的任务清单时，有几点要记住。首先，退一步问问自己：四个象限里都有任务吗？技术负责人在这个练习中最常见的困境之一，就是只填满了上面两个象限，如图 2-3 所示。被问到为什么时，答案几乎总是一样的：“每件事都重要，所以才在我的清单上。”这是“紧急效应”（urgency effect）的经典例子——一种认知偏差：我们倾向于把看似紧急的任务排在优先位置，往往以牺牲那些更重要、但时间上没那么紧迫的工作为代价。一件事感觉很急迫，并不代表它就值得你投入时间和精力。

Let's take a closer look at the board and see what might be moved to the lower quadrants.

我们仔细看看这块看板，想想哪些任务可以被挪到下面两个象限。

Think about the tasks that truly require your unique expertise as a tech lead. Are they things that only you can handle? Some tasks clearly fall into this category, things like showing up for one-on-ones with your team members or joining high-level stakeholder conversations where you're the one who holds the full context. But then there are others. Preparing a demo for a client meeting next week or setting up a demo environment might initially feel like your responsibility, but these are tasks that someone else on your team could take over. By delegating them, you free yourself to focus on what only you can do, and you give others on your team a chance to shine and grow.

想一想，哪些任务真正需要你作为技术负责人的独特专长。哪些是只有你才能处理的？有些任务显然属于这一类，比如出席与团队成员的一对一会议，或加入高层利益相关者对话——在那些对话里，你是唯一掌握完整上下文的人。但还有另一些任务。为下周的客户会议准备演示、或搭建一个演示环境，一开始可能感觉是你的职责，但这些完全可以交给团队里的其他人。把它们委派出去，你就能腾出精力专注于只有你能做的事，也给了团队其他人一个发光和成长的机会。

— PDF p.64 —

Now consider another type of task: the ones you're doing just because it would be nice to have them done. For example, adding an extra level of detail to your system architecture documentation. Sure, you could argue that this is important. But why? Is another team depending on it? Will the product stop working if it's not done? Or is it just that you want everything to be perfectly up-to-date? If the answer to the first two questions is no, and the third one resonates a bit too much, then this is exactly the type of task you can let go of. Move it to the Delegate or Delete quadrant. Let someone else handle it, or let it go altogether.

现在再想想另一类任务：那些你做仅仅是因为“做完了会挺好”的事。比如，给系统架构文档再多加一层细节。当然，你可以争辩说这很重要。但为什么？有别的团队依赖它吗？如果不做，产品就会停摆吗？还是仅仅因为你希望一切都完美地保持最新？如果前两个问题的答案都是“不”，而第三个问题又让你心里咯噔一下，那么这正是那种你可以放手的任务。把它挪到“委派”或“删除”象限。让别人去处理，或者干脆彻底放下。

What happens if I don't do this? This is the key question to ask when looking at tasks like “Color-coding emails,” “Tinkering with low-priority code refactoring that has no current impact,” or “Replacing your current JSON library with a shiny new one.” The honest answer is: probably nothing. These are “nice-to-haves” that often sit on your to-do list but don't add real value. They don't significantly impact your work or your team, and holding onto them just takes up mental space. Move them to the Delete quadrant. If one of these tasks turns out to be really important, it will come back up when it's relevant. Until then, let it go and focus on what matters most.

如果我不做这件事，会怎样？在审视诸如“给邮件按颜色分类”、“琢磨一段眼下毫无影响的低优先级代码重构”、或“把现有的 JSON 库换成一个光鲜亮丽的新库”这类任务时，这是你要问的关键问题。诚实的答案是：很可能什么也不会发生。这些都是“有了更好”的东西，常常挂在你的待办清单上，却不产生真正的价值。它们既不会显著影响你的工作，也不会影响你的团队，攥着不放只会占用你的心智空间。把它们挪到“删除”象限。如果其中某件事事后证明真的重要，等它相关时自然会再次冒出来。在那之前，放下它，专注于最重要的事。

Not having all the quadrants filled in might also be a sign that you're getting stuck in one type of activity, losing track of others, or overlooking blind spots. These blind spots can manifest as areas where you're wasting effort, missing opportunities, or spreading yourself too thin.

并不是每个象限都填满，也可能是一个信号：你正陷在某一类活动里，忽略了其他方面，或没看到自己的盲区。这些盲区可能表现为：你在某些地方白费力气、错失机会，或把自己铺得太开。

If you're spending most of your time in Q1 (Important & Urgent), it's a clear indicator that you're in constant firefighting mode. Things keep popping up unexpectedly, leaving you feeling off guard and reactive. This often means you're not investing enough time in Q2 (Important & Not Urgent), planning and focusing on long-term goals. If you're unsure what to include in Q2, ask your team and your stakeholders: “What should I be focusing on that I'm not?” Their perspective can help uncover opportunities you've overlooked.

如果你把大部分时间花在第一象限（重要且紧急），那是一个明确信号：你正处于持续救火模式。事情不断意外冒出来，让你疲于应对、被动反应。这往往意味着你没有在第二象限（重要但不紧急）投入足够时间——也就是做规划、聚焦长期目标。如果你不确定第二象限该放什么，问问你的团队和利益相关者：“有哪些我本该关注、却没在关注的事？”他们的视角能帮你发现被你忽略的机会。

— PDF p.65 —

On the other hand, spending too much time in Q3 (Urgent & Not Important) suggests you're being distracted by tasks that don't need your direct involvement. These tasks often feel pressing but offer little value. Instead, consider delegating them to your team.

另一方面，如果在第三象限（紧急但不重要）花了太多时间，说明你正被那些并不需要你亲自参与的任务分散精力。这些任务常常感觉很紧迫，却没什么价值。不妨考虑把它们委派给你的团队。

Finally, if you find yourself stuck in Q4 (Not Urgent & Not Important), it's time to reassess. Low-impact tasks might be your way of avoiding more significant challenges. Ask yourself: are you procrastinating on something more meaningful? If so, don't hesitate to reach out for support, whether from your team or peers, and redirect your focus to what's most important.

最后，如果你发现自己陷在第四象限（不紧急也不重要），那就该重新评估了。做低影响的任务，可能是你在逃避更重要的挑战。问问自己：你是不是在拖延某件更有意义的事？如果是，别犹豫，向团队或同事寻求支持，把你的注意力重新导向最重要的事。

By confronting these tendencies, you can move past distractions and focus your energy where it really counts.

直面这些倾向，你就能跨过干扰，把精力集中到真正重要的地方。

Based on this analysis, the board in Figure 2-4 is now much more balanced.

经过这样一番分析，图 2-4 中的看板现在就平衡多了。

While it's not necessary to have tasks in all quadrants, the exercise of filling them all forces you to evaluate the true value of each task and prioritize more effectively. The reality is that you'll likely never finish everything on your to-do list, so making peace with that and learning to delete or let go of less important tasks can help you feel more productive. By clearing away the unnecessary, you'll free yourself from the weight of an overwhelming to-do list and gain the focus needed to concentrate on what matters.

虽然并不需要每个象限都有任务，但把它们都填满这个动作，会迫使你评估每一项任务的真正价值，并更有效地排定优先级。现实是，你很可能永远也做不完待办清单上的所有事，所以坦然接受这一点、学会删除或放下不那么重要的任务，能让你更有效率感。把不必要的东西清掉，你就能从压得人喘不过气的待办清单中解脱出来，重新获得专注于要事所需的精力。

— PDF p.66 —

Step 3: Plan your week第三步：规划你的一周

Once your matrix is filled in, the next step is to extract your key tasks for the upcoming week and map them to specific time slots in your calendar. This is where the magic happens, turning your priorities into a realistic, actionable plan.

矩阵填好之后，下一步是把下周的关键任务抽出来，对应到日历上的具体时间段。神奇之处就发生在这里：你的优先级变成了一份现实、可执行的计划。

Start by asking yourself: does everything fit within your schedule? If not, it's time to reevaluate. Is there something that can be removed or delegated? Be honest about what truly needs your attention and what doesn't. Don't forget to include breaks and some realistic buffer time to account for the inevitable unplanned disruptions that creep in.

先问问自己：这些事都能塞进你的日程吗？如果不能，就该重新评估了。有没有什么可以删掉或委派出去？诚实地判断哪些真的需要你关注、哪些不需要。别忘了留出休息时间和一些现实的缓冲，以应对那些不可避免、悄悄溜进来的计划外干扰。

Planning your week this way gives you a structured approach to your time. It allows you to focus on what matters most and avoid falling into the trap of prioritizing based on “who screams the loudest.” Instead of feeling overwhelmed, you'll feel in control, with a clear plan to tackle the week ahead.

这样规划你的一周，会让你的时间管理有一套结构化的方法。它让你专注于最重要的事，避免掉进“谁叫得最响就先做谁”的陷阱。你不会再感到被压垮，而是会感到一切尽在掌控，带着一份清晰的计划去迎接接下来的一周。

Step 4: Review and adjust第四步：复盘与调整

Reviewing and adjusting your process might feel like just another task on your already overwhelming to-do list, but it's one worth prioritizing. Taking this step helps you uncover patterns, avoid repeating mistakes, and refine a system that becomes more effective over time.

复盘并调整你的流程，可能感觉只是你那已经长得吓人的待办清单上又多了一项，但这一项值得优先安排。迈出这一步，能帮你发现规律、避免重复犯错，并打磨出一套随时间推移越来越有效的体系。

At the end of the week, set aside a few moments to reflect. Consider what urgent issues derailed your plans and whether they were unavoidable. Look at what got deprioritized and ask yourself why. Was it because it wasn't important, or did something else take precedence? Most importantly, think about what you can improve for next week. How much of what you planned did you actually accomplish? If it's around 50%, that's still a solid start. It takes time to get good at planning. Each week gives you a chance to learn and refine your process: Were your estimates off? Did you forget to build in breaks? Did you try to take on too much? Use those insights to tweak your plan for the next week and make it more realistic.

在周末，留出几分钟复盘一下。想想是哪些紧急状况打乱了你的计划，以及它们是否真的不可避免。看看哪些事被降了优先级，问问自己为什么。是因为它本来就不重要，还是因为别的事占了先？最重要的是，想想下周可以改进什么。你计划的事实际完成了多少？如果有 50% 左右，那已经是个不错的开端。做好规划是需要时间的。每一周都给你一次学习和打磨流程的机会：你的预估准不准？是不是忘了留出休息？是不是揽了太多？用这些洞察去微调下周的计划，让它更现实。

Time management tips时间管理小贴士

There are many different time management strategies out there that can help you manage your time as a tech lead, but here are three that I find most effective: time blocking, task batching, and giving myself time to consider whether I can take on a particular task.

市面上有许多不同的时间管理策略能帮技术负责人管好时间，但我发现最有效的有三个：时间块（time blocking）、任务批处理（task batching），以及给自己一点时间来考虑是否能接下某一项任务。

— PDF p.67 —

The first one is time blocking, a simple yet powerful time management method where you allocate specific blocks of time on your calendar for particular tasks or activities. It's about being intentional with your time, ensuring you create space for what matters most, instead of letting your day get hijacked by unplanned distractions. For instance, if you're pairing with team members daily, you can block dedicated hours for pair programming to keep a consistent routine. The same goes for planning: setting aside focus blocks ensures you have uninterrupted time to step back and think strategically. As a tech lead, your team looks to you for direction and long-term planning, not just hands-on coding, so it's crucial to block out time for this.

第一个是时间块。这是一个简单却强大的时间管理方法：在日历上为特定的任务或活动划出专门的时间段。它的核心是有意识地安排时间，确保你为最重要的事留出空间，而不是让计划外的干扰劫持了你一整天。举例来说，如果你每天都和团队成员结对，就可以划出固定的几小时用于结对编程，以保持稳定的节奏。规划也是如此：留出专注时间块，能确保你有不被打断的时间退一步、做战略性思考。作为技术负责人，团队期待你给出方向和长期规划，而不只是动手写代码，因此为这件事留出时间至关重要。

Another effective technique is task batching, which works hand-in-hand with time blocking. Grouping similar tasks, like meetings or feedback sessions, into one block reduces context switching and helps you stay focused.

另一个有效的技巧是任务批处理，它与时间块配合得相得益彰。把类似的任务——比如会议或反馈面谈——归到同一个时间段里，能减少上下文切换，帮你保持专注。

And here's one of my golden rules that helps me protect my schedule: never say yes on the spot. Instead, respond with “Let me think about it,” check your calendar, and make sure it fits.

还有一条我的黄金法则，帮我守护自己的日程：永远不要当场答应。而是回应一句“让我想想”，然后查一下你的日历，确认它排得下。

Time management is about making space for what matters most. By setting weekly intentions, visualizing your workload, prioritizing deliberately, and regularly reviewing and adjusting your plan, you create a system that puts you back in control.

时间管理的本质，是为最重要的事腾出空间。通过设定每周意图、可视化你的工作负荷、审慎地排定优先级，并定期复盘和调整计划，你就搭建起了一套让自己重新掌握主动权的系统。

Avoiding the “Therapist” Trap避开“治疗师”陷阱

One of the most common traps tech leads fall into is trying to solve everyone's problems. Many get into leadership roles because they genuinely want to help others, but this can quickly turn into taking on too much responsibility. What starts with “How can I help?” often turns into “Don't worry, I'll do it for you.”

技术负责人最常掉进的陷阱之一，就是想解决每个人的问题。很多人走上领导岗位，是因为他们真心想帮助别人，但这很快就会变成承担过多责任。以“我能帮你什么？”开场的事，常常会演变成“别担心，我来替你做”。

Note: It's not your job as a tech lead to solve everyone's problems!

注意：作为技术负责人，解决所有人的问题并不是你的职责！

The pitfalls of over-involvement are hard to ignore. Burnout is inevitable if you're constantly stepping in to handle everything (been there, done that). You'll exhaust yourself trying to manage tasks the team should own. Frustration builds quickly too, together with resentment toward the team for not stepping up, toward stakeholders for endless demands, and toward yourself for not setting boundaries.

过度卷入的坑，很难忽视。如果你总是冲上去包办一切，倦怠几乎是必然的（这坑我踩过）。你会累死自己，去管那些本该由团队负责的任务。挫败感也会迅速累积——同时累积的还有怨恨：怨团队不挺身而出，怨利益相关者没完没了地提要求，也怨自己没有设立边界。

— PDF p.68 —

Beyond the individual cost, there's also a hidden team impact: when you always step in, your team misses the chance to develop autonomy. People learn by doing (and struggling) through challenges. If you keep solving problems for them, they won't get the practice or confidence to do it themselves.

除了个人付出的代价，还有一个隐蔽的团队层面的影响：当你总是冲上去时，你的团队就错失了培养自主性的机会。人是通过在挑战中动手（并挣扎）来学习的。如果你一直替他们解决问题，他们就得不到自己动手所需的练习和信心。

And then there's the blame. If you're always the fixer, you become the first to blame when things go wrong. Instead of encouraging shared accountability, you've positioned yourself as the only point of failure.

然后是追责。如果你总是那个“修东西的人”，一旦出问题，你就成了第一个被怪罪的人。你非但没有鼓励共担责任，反而把自己摆成了唯一的故障点。

Early in my career, I fell into this trap when a team member, new to the city, shared his frustrations during a one-on-one. He was struggling to sort out his paperwork, and it was affecting his focus at work. Without even being asked, I jumped in, eager to help. “Don't worry, I'll handle it,” I said, even though I wasn't an expert in the process myself. I took full responsibility: researching the steps, preparing his documents, asking others for advice, and even sitting with him to book his appointments. I even skipped standups to accompany him to appointments.

在我职业生涯早期，我就掉进过这个陷阱。当时一位刚搬到这座城市的团队成员，在一对一沟通中倾诉了他的苦恼。他正为一堆手续文件焦头烂额，这已经影响到他工作时的专注。我甚至没等他开口求我，就迫不及待地跳了进去。“别担心，我来处理。”我说——尽管我自己对这个流程也并不在行。我揽下了全部责任：研究步骤、准备他的材料、向别人请教，甚至陪他一起去预约办理。我还特地缺席了站会陪他去办手续。

It didn't go as planned. We hit roadblocks, and he became increasingly frustrated with me because I hadn't solved it as promised. Meanwhile, I was overwhelmed, my work was suffering, and I felt unappreciated for my efforts. A colleague finally asked me, “Why are you trying so hard to fix his problem? It's not yours to solve.” That moment was a wake-up call. I stepped back, pointed him to someone better suited to help, and let him take over the process. But the damage was done; our professional relationship had soured, and both of us were left feeling frustrated.

事情并没有按计划发展。我们碰到了各种障碍，他对我也越来越不满，因为我并没有像承诺的那样把问题解决掉。与此同时，我自己也被压得喘不过气，本职工作一落千丈，还觉得自己的付出没被领情。终于有位同事问我：“你为什么这么拼命去解决他的问题？这本就不是你该解决的。”那一刻如当头棒喝。我退了一步，把他引荐给更适合帮忙的人，并让他自己接手整个流程。但伤害已经造成：我们的工作关系变了味，两个人都满心挫败。

In hindsight, there were countless moments when I could have handled it differently. Here's how I wish I had approached the situation and how I now tackle similar challenges:

事后回想，有无数个时刻我本可以用不同的方式处理。下面是我希望自己当时那样做的方式，也是我如今应对类似挑战的做法：

Set proper boundaries设立恰当的边界

Before diving into any problem, I take a moment to analyze. In this case, I could've simply said, “I'm sorry to hear that” and taken time to reflect. Was it my problem to solve? No; in fact, he hadn't even explicitly asked for my help. Even if someone does, I now ask myself, “What happens if I say no?” Often, the answer is nothing catastrophic, and the person can handle it with some guidance.

在一头扎进任何问题之前，我会先花一点时间分析。在这件事里，我大可以只说一句“听到这个我很遗憾”，然后花时间反思。这是我该解决的问题吗？不是；事实上，他甚至都没有明确开口求我帮忙。就算有人真的求了，我现在也会先问自己：“如果我说不，会怎样？”通常答案是：不会有什么灾难性后果，而对方在一些指引下完全能自己处理。

Keep yourself in check管好你自己

Reflection is key. Talking it through with a mentor or colleague can offer valuable perspective. Had I done this earlier, I would've realized I was overextending and could've stepped back. I now routinely ask myself, “Are there certain people or tasks draining more of my energy?” or “Am I stepping in when I should be encouraging ownership?”

复盘是关键。和导师或同事把事情聊透，能带来宝贵的视角。如果我早点这么做，就会意识到自己已经用力过猛，本可以退一步。现在我会经常问自己：“是不是某些人或某些任务正在过度消耗我的精力？”或者“我是不是在本该鼓励对方自主负责的时候，却冲上去代劳了？”

— PDF p.69 —

Shift your support转变你的支持方式

Helping doesn't always mean solving. Sometimes it's enough to simply listen: “I'm sorry you're dealing with this.” In other cases, the best move is to point them to someone else. When I finally realized the paperwork wasn't my problem, I identified someone better equipped to help him and sent him their way.

帮助，并不总是意味着替对方解决问题。有时候，仅仅倾听就够了：“很遗憾你要面对这件事。”另一些时候，最好的做法是把他们引荐给别人。当我终于意识到那堆手续文件不是我的问题时，我找到了一位更有能力帮他的人，把他引荐了过去。

The main lesson you can take from this story is to pause before jumping in and ask: Is this problem mine to solve?

从这个故事里，你最该带走的教训是：在冲上去之前先停一下，问问自己——这个问题是该我来解决的吗？

That one question can help you set better boundaries, reduce unnecessary stress, and give the kind of support that's actually needed.

这一个问题，就能帮你设立更好的边界、减少不必要的压力，并给出真正被需要的那种支持。

These lessons apply directly to day-to-day team dynamics. For example, if a team member says, “I can't deal with this task; can you take it over?” my instinct used to be to step in and help. Now, I pause and ask what's making it difficult and how they might approach it differently. Often, with a bit of coaching, they're able to handle it themselves and grow from the experience.

这些教训可以直接应用到日常的团队互动中。比如，当一位团队成员说“我搞不定这个任务，你能接手吗？”，我过去的本能反应是冲上去帮忙。现在，我会先停顿一下，问清楚是什么让它变难、他们又可以换种什么方式来处理。往往，只要稍加引导，他们就能自己搞定，并从这次经历中成长。

It's the same when someone brings me an urgent matter. Before jumping in, I try to understand how urgent it really is by asking, “When do you need an answer?” This gives them a chance to reflect on what they really need and helps you prioritize more intentionally. Often, the request isn't as urgent as it first appears, and they're happy to wait. Sometimes, they might even figure it out themselves before you get to it. But if it is urgent, you can decide whether it truly needs to take priority today. This approach also reduces the chance of people feeling dismissed, as you're making them part of the decision.

当有人拿一件紧急的事来找我时，也是一样。在冲上去之前，我会先问一句“你什么时候需要答案？”，来搞清楚它到底有多急。这给了对方一个机会去想清楚自己真正需要什么，也帮你更有意识地排定优先级。往往，这个请求并不像乍听起来那么紧急，他们也乐于等一等。有时候，他们甚至在你上手之前就自己解决了。但如果它真的紧急，你可以再判断它是否真的需要今天就优先处理。这种做法还能减少让人感觉被敷衍的可能，因为你把他们变成了决策的参与者。

For interpersonal conflict between two team members, don't jump in to mediate right away. Instead, ask each person to give direct feedback to the other and try to find a way to work together. Stepping in too quickly can prevent them from building the skills they need to navigate conflict on their own.

当两位团队成员之间出现人际冲突时，不要马上跳进去当和事佬。相反，请双方直接向对方给出反馈，并尝试找到一种合作共事的方式。介入得太快，会让他们没机会培养自己应对冲突所需的技能。

A helpful lens I use to avoid this trap is to categorize problems into three types:

为了避开这个陷阱，我常用的一个视角是：把问题分成三类：

Problems that are clearly your responsibility明确属于你职责范围的问题

Things like team-wide blockers, technical alignment, or cross-functional miscommunication.

比如团队范围的阻塞问题、技术方向对齐，或跨职能沟通不畅。

— PDF p.70 —

Problems that are clearly their responsibility明确属于对方职责范围的问题

For example, completing a task, owning a feature, or resolving a peer conflict (with your support, not necessarily your intervention).

比如完成一项任务、负责一个功能，或解决一段平级之间的冲突（在你的支持下，但不一定要你亲自介入）。

Gray-area problems灰色地带的问题

Those that could be yours or theirs, depending on the context. In these cases, consider who is best positioned to take ownership based on workload, goals, or development opportunities.

那些既可能是你的、也可能是对方的问题，取决于具体情境。在这种情况下，根据工作量、目标或发展机会，来考虑谁最适合担起这份责任。

This framing helps you slow down before jumping in and makes it easier to coach your team toward ownership instead of taking the reins by default.

这种分类能帮你在冲上去之前慢下来，也更容易引导你的团队走向自主负责，而不是默认由你来掌控一切。

You're part of a team, not a solo problem solver. Set clear boundaries, let others own their responsibilities, and focus on guiding rather than fixing everything yourself. This empowers your team, prevents burnout, and keeps you from being overwhelmed.

你是团队的一员，而不是一个单打独斗的问题解决机器。设立清晰的边界，让别人去扛起他们自己的责任，专注于引导，而不是把一切都自己修好。这会赋能你的团队、防止倦怠，也让你不被压垮。

Avoiding Micromanaging避免微观管理

When I first became a tech lead, I believed micromanagement was the only way to ensure things were done perfectly. I had a to-do list for every person, verified everything they did, and struggled to delegate. I felt constantly angry, frustrated, and ultimately, burned out.

我刚当上技术负责人时，以为微观管理是确保一切完美完成的唯一办法。我给每个人都列了一张待办清单，事无巨细地核查他们做的每一件事，就是学不会委派。我长期处于愤怒、挫败之中，最终 burnout 了。

I learned the hard way that micromanagement isn't sustainable. It limits both the leader and the team, leading to frustration, burnout, and a lack of trust. Micromanaging might feel like control, but it's actually driven by fear: fear that things will go wrong and a lack of trust in both yourself and others.

我吃了苦头才明白，微观管理是不可持续的。它既限制领导者，也限制团队，导致挫败、倦怠和信任缺失。微观管理感觉像是掌控，但它实际上源于恐惧：害怕事情会出岔子，以及对自己和他人都缺乏信任。

The turning point came when I learned to let go. I started by reflecting on my actions, getting feedback, and practicing delegation every day. By doing so, I shifted from trying to control everything to focusing on people and their growth.

转折点出现在我学会放手的时候。我先是反思自己的行为、主动征求反馈，并每天练习委派。这样做之后，我从试图控制一切，转向了关注人、关注他们的成长。

If you recognize yourself in this, it's time to start letting go. Here's how:

如果你在这段描述里看到了自己，是时候开始放手了。方法如下：

Start with small tasks从小任务开始

Delegate small, noncritical tasks first, and trust your team to handle them. Gradually increase responsibility as trust grows. More on this in Chapter 6.

先把一些小的、不关键的任务委派出去，并相信团队能处理好。随着信任加深，逐步增加他们的责任。第 6 章会详细讲这一点。

Give clear expectations, not step-by-step instructions给出清晰的期望，而不是一步步的指令

Focus on the “what,” “why,” and “when” of tasks rather than the “how.” Let your team figure out the most effective way to accomplish tasks. Allow yourself to be surprised by their approach.

关注任务的“做什么”“为什么做”和“什么时候做完”，而不是“怎么做”。让你的团队自己找出最高效的完成方式。允许自己被他们的做法惊喜到。

— PDF p.71 —

Cocreate a tracking system共同搭建一套跟踪系统

Instead of constantly checking in, ask your team to develop a visible tracking process for their progress. Schedule regular check-ins where they report back. This keeps you informed without hovering.

不要不停地去查岗，而是请团队为自己的进度搭建一套可见的跟踪流程。安排定期的 check-in，让他们向你汇报。这样你既掌握情况，又不至于盯得太紧。

Practice saying “I don't know”练习说“我不知道”

Start in a one-on-one with someone you trust, then try it in a team meeting. Notice how it feels and how others respond. It helps build comfort with uncertainty and sets the tone that it's OK not to have all the answers.

先在你信任的人的一对一沟通中试试，然后再在团队会议上尝试。留意它给你的感受，以及别人作何反应。这能帮你逐渐习惯不确定性，并传递一种基调：没有全部答案也没关系。

Admit a mistake承认错误

Pick a comfortable setting, such as a one-on-one, to share a mistake you've made. It's a small but powerful step toward letting go of control.

挑一个让你自在的场合——比如一次一对一——分享你犯过的一个错误。这是朝着放手控制迈出的一小步，却很有力量。

Reflect on your control tendencies反思你的控制倾向

Take time to think about how your need for control impacts your well-being and the people around you. Working with a coach or mentor can offer valuable outside perspective.

花时间想想，你对控制的需求是如何影响你的身心健康、以及你身边的人的。和教练或导师一起合作，能带来宝贵的外部视角。

Ask for help寻求帮助

This requires an extra dose of vulnerability. Let your team in on your journey by admitting, “I've realized I tend to control too much, and I want to work on it. Where do you think I should start?”

这需要多拿出一点勇气示弱。让团队了解你的成长历程，坦诚地说：“我意识到自己控制欲太强了，我想改一改。你们觉得我该从哪里入手？”

When you focus on guiding rather than controlling, your role as a leader becomes about empowering others. This shift benefits your team and your own well-being. You'll have more mental space, less frustration, and greater trust in your team's capabilities.

当你专注于引导而不是控制时，你作为领导者的角色就变成了赋能他人。这个转变既有利于你的团队，也有利于你自己的身心健康。你会有更多的心智空间、更少的挫败感，并对团队的能力有更大的信任。

Micromanagement often comes up as a reason people want to leave their jobs. No one likes to be watched all the time, living with the constant fear of making a mistake and having no autonomy in making their own decisions. As the saying goes, “People leave managers, not jobs.”

微观管理常常成为人们想离职的原因。没人喜欢一直被盯着，活在“怕出错”的持续恐惧里，自己做决定时毫无自主权。正如那句话所说：“人们离开的是经理，而不是工作。”

If you want your team to thrive and stay engaged, invest in building trust. Let them own their tasks, and allow for mistakes, because that's how people learn and grow (e.g., some of the best learnings come from postmortems). You might be surprised at how capable and motivated your team becomes when they feel genuinely trusted and empowered.

如果你想让团队茁壮成长、保持投入，就用心去建立信任。让他们对自己的任务负责，并允许犯错——因为人就是这样学习和成长的（比如，一些最棒的学习就来自事后复盘 postmortem）。当你的团队感受到真正的信任和赋能时，他们会变得多么能干、多么有干劲，你可能会大吃一惊。

Moving away from micromanagement doesn't mean losing control of outcomes; it's about gaining trust and respect. You'll see results not by doing everything yourself but by leveraging the full potential of your team. It's a shift from “I must do everything to make sure it's perfect” to “I trust my team to succeed, and together we'll grow.”

摆脱微观管理，并不意味着对结果失去掌控；它关乎赢得信任和尊重。你看到成果，不是靠自己包办一切，而是靠充分发挥团队的潜力。这是一种转变：从“我必须亲力亲为才能确保完美”，转向“我信任我的团队能成功，我们会一起成长”。

— PDF p.72 —

Balancing Building and Leading在动手构建与带领团队之间取得平衡

Another challenge for tech leads is deciding how much time to spend coding versus overseeing technical decisions.

技术负责人面临的另一个挑战，是决定花多少时间写代码、又花多少时间把控技术决策。

When I first became a tech lead, I found myself naturally drawn to high-level strategy and discussions, leaving less time for hands-on coding. I enjoyed meetings, brainstorming solutions, and setting direction for the team, but I soon realized I was losing touch with the actual technical work.

我刚当上技术负责人时，发现自己天生就被高层战略和各种讨论所吸引，留给动手写代码的时间越来越少。我喜欢开会、头脑风暴解决方案、为团队设定方向，但很快我就意识到，自己正在和实际的技术工作脱节。

At the same time, I've also met tech leads who remain deeply immersed in coding, losing sight of the bigger picture because transitioning to a leadership role feels unfamiliar and uncomfortable. Both approaches come with their own set of challenges.

但与此同时，我也遇到过另一些技术负责人，他们深深沉浸在写代码里，因为转型到领导岗位让他们感到陌生、不自在，结果反而失去了对全局的把握。这两种做法各有各的一系列挑战。

Determining where you fall on the spectrum between technical and organizational focus starts with honest self-reflection. Imagine a day where you could choose to do only one thing. Would you rather spend it immersed in code, building and debugging, or would you lean toward conversations, planning, and driving strategic direction for your team? Your answers to these questions can reveal where your strengths and interests naturally lie, helping you align your focus as a tech lead.

要判断自己在“技术专注”与“组织专注”这个光谱上处于哪个位置，要从诚实的自我反思开始。想象有这么一天，你只能选择做一件事。你更愿意沉浸在代码里、构建和调试，还是更倾向于讨论、规划、为团队推动战略方向？你对这些问题的回答，能揭示你的优势和兴趣天然偏向哪里，帮你作为技术负责人校准自己的焦点。

Recognizing your natural tendencies is important, but to be a successful tech lead, you need to have the ability to switch gears between hands-on coding and strategic oversight based on what your team and project need most.

认清自己的天然倾向很重要，但要成为一名成功的技术负责人，你还需要具备这样一种能力：根据团队和项目最需要什么，在动手写代码与战略把控之间切换挡位。

If you're too focused on coding, it might show up in a few ways. Maybe you're the first to jump on every pull request or technical challenge, leaving little room for others to step in. You might know the codebase inside out, while the rest of the team feels left out of key decisions. If you're skipping meetings or high-level planning, chances are the team is missing the clear direction they need to move forward.

如果你过于专注写代码，可能会有一些表现。也许每个 pull request、每个技术挑战你都是第一个扑上去的，几乎没给别人留下介入的空间。你可能对代码库了如指掌，而团队其他人却感觉被排除在关键决策之外。如果你老是缺席会议或高层规划，那团队很可能正缺少前进所需的清晰方向。

On the flip side, being too focused on oversight can leave you feeling disconnected from the code. You might find yourself zoning out in standups or struggling to understand the technical details the team is discussing. This can frustrate your team when they are discussing technical problems and you're either unavailable or too out of touch to step in.

反过来，过于专注于把控，会让你感觉和代码断了联系。你可能会在站会上走神，或费力去理解团队正在讨论的技术细节。当团队在讨论技术问题时，如果你要么没空、要么脱节到插不上手，这会让他们很受挫。

The key to being an effective tech lead is adaptability. You'll need to adjust your focus based on the project phase and your team's needs. For example:

做一名高效技术负责人的关键，是适应性。你需要根据项目阶段和团队的需求来调整你的焦点。例如：

— PDF p.73 —
  • When deadlines are tight, you might need to dive into the code and work alongside your team.当截止日期很紧时，你可能需要扎进代码里，和团队并肩作战。
  • When there's a new feature to plan, you might spend more time away from coding, working with stakeholders and aligning the team on the strategy.当有新功能要规划时，你可能需要少写代码，多和利益相关者协作、让团队在战略上对齐。

Here are some practical tips for finding balance:

下面是一些找到平衡的实用建议：

Block time for both为两者都留出时间

Schedule coding and pair programming blocks into your calendar while keeping time open for meetings, reviews, and strategy sessions. This ensures you're hands-on without losing sight of the bigger picture.

在日历上安排写代码和结对编程的时间块，同时也留出时间给会议、评审和战略讨论。这样能确保你既动手实践，又不迷失于全局。

Delegate but stay informed委派出去，但保持知情

You don't need to be the one writing every line of code, but stay involved enough to guide technical discussions and ensure the code quality is up to standards.

你不需要每一行代码都自己写，但要足够地参与其中，以便引导技术讨论、确保代码质量达到标准。

Engage in code reviews参与代码评审

Even if you can't contribute code regularly, reviewing pull requests (PRs) is a great way to stay connected to the technical aspects without being fully hands-on. I also know tech leads who do PR reviews every morning with the team, all together, not as a line-by-line review but more as a high-level walkthrough, scrolling through the code to share insights and context. If you work with trunk-based development and have no PRs, block core pair programming hours on your calendar.

即使你不能经常性地贡献代码，评审 pull request（PR）也是一个好办法，让你不必全程动手也能和技术层面保持联系。我还认识一些技术负责人，每天早上和团队一起做 PR 评审——不是逐行评审，而更像是一场高层级的走读，一起滚动浏览代码、分享洞见和上下文。如果你采用的是 trunk-based 开发、没有 PR，那就在日历上划出核心的结对编程时间。

Ask for feedback征求反馈

Check with your team and your stakeholders to see if they feel you're striking the right balance. They'll let you know if they need more of your technical input or if they feel you're too involved.

和你的团队、利益相关者确认一下，看看他们觉得你是否找到了恰当的平衡。如果你需要更多技术投入、或者他们觉得你管得太多，他们会告诉你的。

The key to overcoming this challenge is to remain flexible. Some phases of a project will demand more hands-on coding, while others require you to step back and focus on guiding your team. The goal isn't to be perfect in both areas but to adapt to what the situation calls for and ensure you're meeting both the technical and leadership needs of your team.

克服这个挑战的关键，是保持灵活。项目的某些阶段会需要更多动手写代码，而另一些阶段则需要你退一步、专注于引导团队。目标不是在两方面都做到完美，而是适应形势所需，并确保你同时满足团队在技术和领导两方面的需求。

— PDF p.74 —

Key Takeaway本章要点

Stepping into the tech lead role can feel overwhelming, but it becomes much more manageable when you approach it intentionally. This chapter was about giving you a structure to grow in a way that fits you. From clarifying what's expected to figuring out where you're starting from, it's all about creating a path you can actually follow.

走上技术负责人岗位可能会让你觉得压力山大，但当你有意识地去应对时，它就变得可控多了。本章的主旨，是给你一套结构，让你以适合自己的方式成长。从厘清期望，到摸清自己的起点，这一切都是为了为你规划出一条真正走得通的路。

You don't need to get it all right immediately. What matters is that you keep learning, adjusting, and showing up with purpose.

你不需要一下子就把一切做对。重要的是持续学习、不断调整，并带着目标感出现在每一个当下。
